title: What a Home Appraisal Does in a California Purchase Transaction
content_html:
If you're financing a home purchase in California, a home appraisal will almost certainly be part of your transaction. It's a step that often gets mentioned quickly in a purchase agreement but misunderstood by buyers until it actually happens. Here's a plain-language look at what an appraisal is, who orders it, what the appraiser is actually evaluating, and what happens when the number that comes back doesn't match the purchase price.

What Is a Home Appraisal?

A home appraisal is an independent, professional opinion of a property's market value, performed by a licensed or certified appraiser. In a purchase transaction, the appraisal exists primarily to protect the lender: before a bank or mortgage company agrees to loan money secured by a property, it wants assurance that the property is actually worth what's being paid for it. If a loan ever went into default, the lender needs to know the collateral is sufficient to recover its investment.

This is different from a home inspection, which evaluates the physical condition of systems and components in the home. An appraisal is concerned with value, not condition in the same granular sense — though condition does factor into the value opinion.

Who Orders the Appraisal, and Who Picks the Appraiser

The lender orders the appraisal, not the buyer and not the real estate agent. Federal and state rules require lenders to use an independent appraisal management process so the appraiser's opinion isn't influenced by anyone with a financial stake in the deal closing. In practice, the buyer typically pays the appraisal fee as part of closing costs, but the lender selects the appraiser, usually through an appraisal management company, and the buyer's agent and seller's agent have no say in who is assigned.

What the Appraiser Actually Evaluates

An appraiser visits the property and prepares a written report, most commonly using a standardized form for single-family homes. The process generally includes:

  • A physical inspection of the property — square footage, number of bedrooms and bathrooms, lot size, condition of visible systems, upgrades, and any obvious defects.
  • A comparable sales analysis — the appraiser researches recently sold homes in the same area that are similar in size, age, condition, and features, then adjusts for differences (a pool, an extra bedroom, a larger lot) to arrive at an estimated market value.
  • Neighborhood and market factors — general trends in the area, marketability, and anything that could affect resale value.

The appraiser is not evaluating the buyer's taste in the home or how much the buyer wants it — only what comparable, arm's-length sales support as fair market value at that point in time.

Why the Purchase Price and the Appraised Value Can Differ

In a competitive market, buyers sometimes agree to a purchase price that exceeds recent comparable sales — for example, in a multiple-offer situation. The appraisal doesn't know or care what the buyer offered; it's based on what similar homes have actually sold for. When the appraisal comes in at or above the purchase price, nothing changes — the transaction proceeds as planned. When it comes in below the purchase price, that's commonly called an "appraisal gap," and it creates a decision point for both sides.

What Happens When an Appraisal Comes in Low

A lender generally will not loan more than a set percentage of the appraised value, not the purchase price, when the two differ. That leaves a few possible paths, depending on what the purchase agreement allows and what the parties agree to:

  • The buyer covers the difference in cash — paying the gap between the loan amount the lender will approve and the agreed purchase price out of pocket.
  • The seller lowers the price — bringing the purchase price down to match the appraised value, which is often negotiated when the seller wants the deal to proceed.
  • Both sides split the difference — a negotiated middle ground.
  • The buyer challenges the appraisal — requesting a reconsideration of value if there's reason to believe the appraiser missed relevant comparable sales or made an error. This isn't guaranteed to change the outcome.
  • The deal falls through — if a purchase agreement includes an appraisal contingency, the buyer typically has the right to cancel and recover their deposit if the appraisal comes in low and the parties can't reach another resolution.

Whether any of these paths is available in a given transaction depends heavily on how the purchase agreement was written, so it's worth understanding contingencies before making an offer, not after an appraisal comes back.

Cash Transactions and Appraisals

Because the appraisal exists primarily for the lender's benefit, a cash buyer isn't required to get one. Some cash buyers choose to order an appraisal anyway as a value check, but it's optional rather than a built-in step the way it is in a financed purchase.

Appraisal Timing in the Transaction

The appraisal is typically ordered early in escrow, often around the same time as the home inspection, since both can affect whether and how the deal moves forward. The appraiser needs access to the home, so sellers should expect a scheduled visit similar to an inspection appointment. Turnaround time for the written report varies by appraiser workload and property complexity, so buyers and agents should build some cushion into the closing timeline rather than assuming it will be back within a specific number of days.

What an Appraisal Does Not Do

It's worth being clear about the limits of an appraisal. It does not replace a home inspection and shouldn't be relied on to catch every physical defect. It does not guarantee the home will sell for that value in the future — value opinions reflect a point in time. And it does not obligate the lender to approve the loan on its own; the appraisal is one piece of the overall underwriting process alongside the buyer's credit, income, and other financial factors.

Why This Matters for Buyers and Sellers

For buyers, understanding the appraisal process means going into an offer — especially a competitive one — with a realistic sense of what happens if the number comes in below the agreed price, and making sure the purchase agreement addresses that scenario before it's needed. For sellers, it means being prepared for a lender-ordered appraisal to test whether the agreed price holds up against recent comparable sales, which is one more reason accurate, well-supported pricing matters from the start. Both sides benefit from working through these scenarios with their agent before they become live issues mid-escrow.
